_comment: Per-language security tools `sv` can run, described here rather than in Rust, so adding one is a data change. Three rules shape every entry. First, SARIF only: each tool is asked for SARIF 2.1.0 and nothing else, because one output parser that is trusted is worth more than five that are nearly right, and a tool that cannot emit SARIF is simply not listed yet. Second, a tool that is not installed reports NOT RUN and how to install it — never a clean pass, which is the whole reason this file exists rather than a shell script. Third, `rules` maps the tool's own rule ids to requirements one at a time. A blanket list per tool would credit bandit's SQL rule with everything bandit knows about; a finding whose rule id is not in the map carries no requirement at all, which is a fair thing to be and is shown as such.

adapters.name: Bandit
adapters.note: Bandit has no SARIF formatter of its own; `bandit-sarif-formatter` registers one, which is why the install line names two packages. Bandit installed without it exits with `invalid choice: 'sarif'` and writes nothing, which is reported as not run with that message attached rather than as a clean scan. Bandit also exits non-zero when it finds something, which is not a failure to run: only a missing report counts as that.

adapters.name: gosec
adapters.note: gosec resolves `./...` against the working directory, so it is run from inside the app folder rather than given a path.

adapters.name: Brakeman
adapters.note: Brakeman only understands Rails applications. On a Ruby app that is not Rails it exits without a report, which is recorded as not run rather than as nothing found.

adapters.name: Semgrep
adapters.note: The only entry that reads more than one language, and the only one that fetches its rules from the network the first time it runs. `sv` itself opens no connection; this tool does, which is why it is listed with that said rather than left to be discovered.
